title: When to Stop Penalizing Actions? Martingale GRPO for VLA Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: When to Stop Penalizing Actions? Martingale GRPO for VLA Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract A failed vision-language-action (VLA) rollout does not imply that every action contributed to failure.
Yet in group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), a single trajectory-level advantage is assigned to all actions in a rollout.
Potentially useful recovery attempts can thus be penalized alongside the errors they aim to correct.
Ideal stopping conditions for failure feedback are characterized using success-probability and policy-score martingales.
At these stops, the removed gradient contribution has zero conditional expectation given the retained information.
Truncation therefore preserves the expectation of a reference GRPO group-gradient estimator and can reduce its covariance.
One such stop occurs when the conditional probability of success is zero, motivating error and recovery cues for selecting candidate feedback boundaries.
Martingale GRPO ( MART-GRPO ) is introduced with a vision-language model (VLM) for event-guided truncation.
The VLM is fine-tuned on our annotated training set using low-rank adaptation (LoRA).
The last visible error without observed recovery is localized by the frozen VLM in complete rollout videos.
Failure feedback is retained through the selected error interval and removed afterward, while successful-rollout loss terms and original loss normalization are preserved.
For retrospective boundaries, changes in expectation and variance are analyzed to assess departures from ideal stopping.
Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on RoboTwin 2.0 show that MART-GRPO improves success rates over full-trajectory GRPO across multiple tasks.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to actions ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025b ) . Pretrained policies are adapted through supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations ( Kim et al., 2025a ) and further optimized through reinforcement learning from environment interaction ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) turns terminal task rewards into trajectory-level advantages by comparing rollouts collected for the same task. Each advantage is then applied across the rollout’s action chunks. A terminal failure does not imply that every action contributed to failure. For example, a policy may drop an object, attempt to regrasp it, and exhaust its interaction budget (Figure 1 ). In a mixed-outcome group, the failed rollout’s negative advantage penalizes both the error and the subsequent recovery attempts. This motivates the question: When to stop penalizing actions? Figure 1: Errors and recovery attempts within a failed rollout. Selected RoboTwin hammer frames from two scenes, a success (top) and a failure (bottom). The red outline marks the hammer after it is lost at chunk 2, and the later frames show recovery attempts. In mixed-outcome groups, full GRPO assigns the error and subsequent recovery attempts the same negative advantage. Several methods already change which actions receive feedback, each at a different point in the pipeline. Temporal GRPO reconstructs stage-relative advantages but requires task-stage detection and rollout alignment ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) . PCM allocates gradient computation through chunk sampling guided by phase-level success–failure divergence ( Bagaria et al., 2026 ) . RedFlow’s corrective targets require suitable successful matches in offline data ( Yan et al., 2026 ) . In LLM reinforcement learning, negative-advantage updates are masked in μ \mu -GRPO using importance-ratio triggers ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . ESPO terminates rollouts early ( Li et al., 2026b ) , whereas PS-PPO samples update prefixes with importance weighting to preserve the reference gradient expectation ( Hwang & Kim, 2026 ) . Here, failed-rollout suffixes are masked using visible errors and recovery cues after complete execution. Group advantages and original loss normalization are retained without additional correction weights for truncation. To identify a principled truncation boundary, we ask when future actions make no expected gradient contribution. At a fixed policy, the conditional success probability and the cumulative policy score are both martingales, and their increments carry that contribution. Together they define the remaining conditional credit : the expected policy-gradient contribution of future actions given the observed history. For example, when failure is already determined by the observed history, the remaining credit is zero. If the decision to stop reads only the observed prefix and the remaining credit is zero, the removed failure contribution has zero conditional expectation. For conditionally independent rollouts whose normalization factors are measurable with respect to the retained information, the truncated GRPO group-gradient estimator is a conditional projection of the full reference estimator. It therefore has the same expectation and no greater covariance. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Martingale GRPO ( MART-GRPO ) for event-guided failure-feedback selection. A vision-language model (VLM) selects feedback boundaries based on visible errors and whether recovery follows. The VLM is fine-tuned on error and recovery annotations and frozen during policy optimization. It reads each complete failed rollout and localizes the onset of the last visible error without observed recovery to a chunk interval. Later frames help interpret earlier events, so the boundary is selected retrospectively. The interval’s right endpoint defines B B : failure feedback is retained from chunk 0 0 through B B and removed afterward. Successful-rollout loss terms are retained. A conditional residual relates these retrospective boundaries to the conditional projection above and bounds their effects on gradient expectation and total variance. Our contributions are threefold. • A martingale analysis of failure feedback. Ideal stopping rules are characterized through remaining conditional credit and a conditional projection of the complete GRPO group-gradient estimator. The projection preserves the reference expectation without increasing covariance, while residual and bias–variance analyses characterize the effects of retrospective boundaries. • Event-guided feedback truncation with MART-GRPO . A VLM is fine-tuned with LoRA on our annotated training set and frozen to localize the last visible error without observed recovery in complete rollouts. These event intervals are converted into failure-prefix masks that preserve successful-rollout loss terms, group advantages, and original loss normalization. • Empirical evaluation of policy performance and feedback selection. Seven-task OpenVLA-OFT comparisons on RoboTwin 2.0 show higher mean success than Full GRPO, complemented by localization and feedback-use measurements. Two-task ablations favor event-guided truncation over uniform penalty scaling and random prefixes.

Under the conditions below, removing a contribution with zero conditional expectation given the retained information preserves the full-feedback estimator’s expectation without increasing covariance. Two martingales make this statement precise for GRPO, and a projection residual then covers boundaries selected from complete rollouts.

sections.text: Failure certification motivates looking for errors after which recovery is unlikely within the remaining budget. Visible errors and recovery observations serve as cues for candidate boundaries, whose statistical effects are characterized below.

sections.heading: 3 Martingale GRPO
sections.text: Section 2 identifies conditions for preserving the reference gradient expectation when removing a failure suffix. The failure-certification case (Corollary 3 ) motivates using visible errors and recovery as cues for candidate boundaries. MART-GRPO retains feedback on localized errors and uses subsequent recovery observations to select the suffix to mask (Figure 3 ). A frozen VLM reviews each complete failed rollout and localizes the last visible error without observed recovery. A fixed mapping converts this interval into a failure-prefix mask for GRPO. sections.heading: Event supervision.
sections.text: The VLM input x x combines task instructions, three synchronized camera views, proprioceptive observations, and frame-to-chunk alignment. Structured targets record visible outcomes, error types, localization intervals, supporting frames, and observed recovery. The interval brackets the onset of the target error, since its exact chunk is uncertain. The corpus contains 1,024 failed rollout videos with event annotations, supplemented by successful reference videos. Training, validation, and test partitions have disjoint task–scene identities. Annotation details and split counts are documented in Appendix E .

sections.text: The VLM uses later observations to interpret errors and recovery, so B B is retrospective. Proposition 4 characterizes these masks through a conditional projection residual. For these boundaries, the ideal projection guarantee requires η B = 0 \eta_{B}=0 , an additional condition beyond visible-event localization. Policy comparisons in Section 4 assess learning under the clipped PPO objective.

sections.heading: 4 Evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate VLM event localization, VLA policy performance, and two ablations on the amount and temporal placement of failure feedback.

sections.heading: 4.1 VLM event localization
sections.text: We evaluate 220 unrecovered test failures with annotated intervals from the seven policy tasks, using the task–scene-disjoint split in Section 3 . Interval intersection-over-union (IoU) compares discrete chunk sets. Endpoint accuracy measures agreement within a given chunk distance of the annotated right endpoint. Both metrics use predictions before semantic fallback, score missing intervals as zero, and average within tasks and then across tasks. Validation IoU selects update 304 (epoch 8). These scores measure exploratory agreement with the reference annotations (Appendix E.3 ). Figure 4 compares the base model with epochs 3, 6, and 8. Task-macro IoU rises from 28.5 % 28.5\% to 50.9 % 50.9\% , 67.8 % 67.8\% , and 72.1 % 72.1\% , respectively. The selected checkpoint achieves 68.1 % 68.1\% exact endpoint agreement and 91.8 % 91.8\% agreement within one chunk. Per-task values appear in Table 8 . Figure 4: VLM event localization. sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We compare SFT, Full GRPO, and MART-GRPO on seven RoboTwin 2.0 tasks ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , using the action-token implementation of OpenVLA-OFT from SimpleVLA-RL ( Kim et al., 2025a ; Li et al., 2026a ) . Both RL methods start from the same task-specific SFT checkpoint. Each update uses 64 accepted groups of eight rollouts, mixed-outcome filtering with adaptive refill, global PPO minibatch 128, and the original token normalization. The actor receives a head-camera view and proprioception, while the frozen VLM reviews three views. Experiments run on servers equipped with eight H100 GPUs. Greedy evaluation uses 128 training-seed (Seen) and 128 held-out-seed episodes under the same task configuration every five updates. The primary endpoint is update 40. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: We study where failure feedback should end in VLA reinforcement learning. Two martingales characterize remaining conditional credit and identify ideal stops that preserve the reference group-gradient expectation without increasing covariance. Guided by this analysis, MART-GRPO selects feedback boundaries from visible errors and recovery in complete rollout videos. Retrospective residuals characterize departures of these boundaries from the ideal projection. Policy evaluations show success-rate improvements over Full GRPO across multiple tasks. On both ablation tasks, VLM-guided truncation achieves higher endpoint success than uniform penalty scaling and random prefix selection. A key open question is how reliably visible events track remaining credit as the policy evolves. Future work will examine this relationship across policy stages and develop prefix-based event predictors.

sections.heading: VLA models and reinforcement learning.
sections.text: Vision-language pretraining supports robot control in RT-2 and OpenVLA ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025b ) , while π 0 \pi_{0} uses flow-based continuous action generation ( Black et al., 2025 ) . OpenVLA-OFT studies efficient supervised adaptation ( Kim et al., 2025a ) . VLA-RL and SimpleVLA-RL develop RL pipelines for pretrained policies ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026a ) , with further work examining RL generalization ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . We select which action chunks receive terminal failure feedback while retaining the policy architecture and environment reward.

sections.heading: Temporal credit assignment.
sections.text: RUDDER redistributes delayed rewards through return prediction ( Arjona-Medina et al., 2019 ) . Hindsight and counterfactual credit assignment use future information to construct action-credit estimates or baselines ( Harutyunyan et al., 2019 ; Mesnard et al., 2021 ) . Temporal GRPO reconstructs stage-relative advantages using task-stage detection and rollout alignment, while GiGPO estimates local credit at repeated anchor states ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . These methods build a new credit signal. We keep the existing trajectory-level advantage and change only the actions it reaches.

sections.heading: Truncating negative feedback.
sections.text: A second group changes which update terms survive. PCM samples chunks using phase-level success–failure divergence to allocate gradient computation ( Bagaria et al., 2026 ) . μ \mu -GRPO uses importance-ratio triggers to veto suffix updates, motivated by off-policy prefix mismatch ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . ESPO uses a regret surrogate to terminate failing rollouts early and assign terminal failure ( Li et al., 2026b ) , whereas PS-PPO samples update prefixes with importance weighting to preserve the reference gradient expectation and study the variance–computation tradeoff ( Hwang & Kim, 2026 ) . MART-GRPO masks failed-rollout suffixes after complete execution, selecting boundaries from visible errors and recovery. Existing group advantages and loss normalization are retained without additional truncation correction weights.

sections.heading: Vision-language feedback and corrective learning.
sections.text: Vision-language feedback has been used to construct rewards from image–text similarity ( Rocamonde et al., 2024 ) , video or textual demonstrations ( Sontakke et al., 2023 ) , and process-level predictions ( Lu et al., 2025 ) . REFLECT summarizes robot experiences for failure explanation and correction ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . DLS uses privileged simulator states for progress-localized signals and directional shaping in flow-based VLA adaptation ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . RedFlow estimates chunk quality and derives corrective action targets from successful matches in offline data ( Yan et al., 2026 ) . In MART-GRPO , the fine-tuned VLM identifies the last visible error without observed recovery in complete videos. Its interval selects where an existing negative advantage ends, while the scalar task reward remains unchanged.

sections.heading: Gradient variance and normalization.
sections.text: REINFORCE and the policy-gradient theorem give the score-function foundation ( Williams, 1992 ; Sutton et al., 1999 ) . Baselines and value-based advantage estimates address gradient variance ( Greensmith et al., 2004 ; Schulman et al., 2016 ) , while GRPO and RLOO use groups of sampled outcomes ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) . Dr. GRPO analyzes normalization bias, and DAPO studies token-level aggregation and dynamic sampling ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . These loss and normalization choices affect the reference update itself. We characterize failure-only truncation of complete GRPO groups through optional sampling and conditional-expectation projection ( Durrett, 2019 ) . The analysis covers dependent advantages, token denominators, and outcome filtering. Under the stopping and measurability conditions, the projection preserves the reference expectation without increasing covariance. This guarantee concerns the reference estimator before PPO clipping ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . Conditional projection residuals characterize expectation and variance changes under retrospective boundary selection.

sections.text: A shared template combines the task instruction and a fixed task-specific clarification with the executed chunk count, initial action budget, and synchronized observations. The clarification specifies the intended manipulation, such as stacking the bowls and releasing the moved bowl. The system instruction and an abridged version of the user instruction are shown below. VLM event-localization prompt System instruction. Review robot video evidence. Return the requested concise JSON. User instruction (abridged). Review the synchronized camera views and robot observations for the given task. Track objects across views and check whether apparent errors are followed by regrasping or task completion. Identify the last visible error sequence without subsequent recovery and localize its onset using the recorded frame-to-chunk mapping. Return a chunk interval when timing is ambiguous and a null interval when no specific error can be localized. Required response. Return a compact JSON response containing the observed outcome, grasp and handover status, error type, error interval, recovery status, final holder, up to six supporting frame indices, and a brief factual summary. Frozen-model inference uses greedy decoding with at most 512 generated tokens. The resulting event record supplies the outcome, interval, and recovery information used by the boundary rule.

sections.heading: Boundary mapping and fallbacks.
sections.text: The mapping in Equations 13 and 14 is applied in the following order. 1. Select rollouts. Terminal environment rewards determine which rollouts require inference. Failed rollouts are passed to the event model, while successful rollouts bypass it and retain all their loss terms. 2. Validate responses. The mapper checks the response schema and any non-null interval. A valid interval contains two integer chunk indices satisfying 0 ≤ ℓ i ≤ u i < K i 0\leq\ell_{i}\leq u_{i}<K_{i} . Malformed responses, identity mismatches, and failed inference requests raise implementation errors rather than becoming no-event predictions. 3. Apply semantic fallbacks. Full feedback is retained for a predicted success or uncertain outcome, no clear error, an uncertain error type, or a missing localization interval. It is also retained when subsequent recovery from the localized error is reported or uncertain. 4. Set the boundary. For a valid failure prediction with a localized error and no observed recovery, the mapper returns the upper interval endpoint as B i = u i B_{i}=u_{i} . Supporting frame identifiers provide evidence for inspection. The validated event fields determine the feedback boundary.

Martingale GRPO for VLA Reinforcement Learning Zongyao Zhao, Cheng-Jie Zhao, Ruihang Jiang, Bing Zheng, Zhaolin Wang, Yuanwei Liu Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong Affiliation: Tsinghua University Abstract A failed vision-language-action (VLA) rollout does not imply that every action contributed to failure. Yet in group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), a single trajectory-level advantage is assigned to all actions in a rollout. Potentially useful recovery attempts can thus be penalized alongside the errors they aim to correct. Ideal stopping conditions for failure feedback are characterized using success-probability and policy-score martingales. At these stops, the removed gradient contribution has zero conditional expectation given the retained information. Truncation therefore preserves the expectation of a reference GRPO group-gradient estimator and can reduce its covariance. One such stop occurs when the conditional probability of success is zero, motivating error and recovery cues for selecting candidate feedback boundaries. Martingale GRPO ( MART-GRPO ) is introduced with a vision-language model (VLM) for event-guided truncation. The VLM is fine-tuned on our annotated training set using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The last visible error without observed recovery is localized by the frozen VLM in complete rollout videos. Failure feedback is retained through the selected error interval and removed afterward, while successful-rollout loss terms and original loss normalization are preserved. For retrospective boundaries, changes in expectation and variance are analyzed to assess departures from ideal stopping. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on RoboTwin 2.0 show that MART-GRPO improves success rates over full-trajectory GRPO across multiple tasks. 1 Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to actions ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025b ) . Pretrained policies are adapted through supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations ( Kim et al., 2025a ) and further optimized through reinforcement learning from environment interaction ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) turns terminal task rewards into trajectory-level advantages by comparing rollouts collected for the same task. Each advantage is then applied across the rollout’s action chunks. A terminal failure does not imply that every action contributed to failure. For example, a policy may drop an object, attempt to regrasp it, and exhaust its interaction budget (Figure 1 ). In a mixed-outcome group, the failed rollout’s negative advantage penalizes both the error and the subsequent recovery attempts. This motivates the question: When to stop penalizing actions? Figure 1: Errors and recovery attempts within a failed rollout. Selected RoboTwin hammer frames from two scenes, a success (top) and a failure (bottom). The red outline marks the hammer after it is lost at chunk 2, and the later frames show recovery attempts. In mixed-outcome groups, full GRPO assigns the error and subsequent recovery attempts the same negative advantage. Several methods already change which actions receive feedback, each at a different point in the pipeline. Temporal GRPO reconstructs stage-relative advantages but requires task-stage detection and rollout alignment ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) . PCM allocates gradient computation through chunk sampling guided by phase-level success–failure divergence ( Bagaria et al., 2026 ) . RedFlow’s corrective targets require suitable successful matches in offline data ( Yan et al., 2026 ) . In LLM reinforcement learning, negative-advantage updates are masked in μ \mu -GRPO using importance-ratio triggers ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . ESPO terminates rollouts early ( Li et al., 2026b ) , whereas PS-PPO samples update prefixes with importance weighting to preserve the reference gradient expectation ( Hwang & Kim, 2026 ) . Here, failed-rollout suffixes are masked using visible errors and recovery cues after complete execution. Group advantages and original loss normalization are retained without additional correction weights for truncation. To identify a principled truncation boundary, we ask when future actions make no expected gradient contribution. At a fixed policy, the conditional success probability and the cumulative policy score are both martingales, and their increments carry that contribution. Together they define the remaining conditional credit : the expected policy-gradient contribution of future actions given the observed history. For example, when failure is already determined by the observed history, the remaining credit is zero. If the decision to stop reads only the observed prefix and the remaining credit is zero, the removed failure contribution has zero conditional expectation. For conditionally independent rollouts whose normalization factors are measurable with respect to the retained information, the truncated GRPO group-gradient estimator is a conditional projection of the full reference estimator. It therefore has the same expectation and no greater covariance. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Martingale GRPO ( MART-GRPO ) for event-guided failure-feedback selection. A vision-language model (VLM) selects feedback boundaries based on visible errors and whether recovery follows. The VLM is fine-tuned on error and recovery annotations and frozen during policy optimization. It reads each complete failed rollout and localizes the onset of the last visible error without observed recovery to a chunk interval. Later frames help interpret earlier events, so the boundary is selected retrospectively. The interval’s right endpoint defines B B : failure feedback is retained from chunk 0 0 through B B and removed afterward. Successful-rollout loss terms are retained. A conditional residual relates these retrospective boundaries to the conditional projection above and bounds their effects on gradient expectation and total variance. Our contributions are threefold. • A martingale analysis of failure feedback. Ideal stopping rules are characterized through remaining conditional credit and a conditional projection of the complete GRPO group-gradient estimator. The projection preserves the reference expectation without increasing covariance, while residual and bias–variance analyses characterize the effects of retrospective boundaries. • Event-guided feedback truncation with MART-GRPO . A VLM is fine-tuned with LoRA on our annotated training set and frozen to localize the last visible error without observed recovery in complete rollouts. These event intervals are converted into failure-prefix masks that preserve successful-rollout loss terms, group advantages, and original loss normalization. • Empirical evaluation of policy performance and feedback selection. Seven-task OpenVLA-OFT comparisons on RoboTwin 2.0 show higher mean success than Full GRPO, complemented by localization and feedback-use measurements. Two-task ablations favor event-guided truncation over uniform penalty scaling and random prefixes. 2 A Martingale Analysis of Failure Feedback We analyze feedback truncation through the gradient contribution of the discarded suffix. Success after 40 updates, with SFT references and task-specific horizontal scales. 5 Conclusion and Limitations We study where failure feedback should end in VLA reinforcement learning. Two martingales characterize remaining conditional credit and identify ideal stops that preserve the reference group-gradient expectation without increasing covariance. Guided by this analysis, MART-GRPO selects feedback boundaries from visible errors and recovery in complete rollout videos. Retrospective residuals characterize departures of these boundaries from the ideal projection. Policy evaluations show success-rate improvements over Full GRPO across multiple tasks. On both ablation tasks, VLM-guided truncation achieves higher endpoint success than uniform penalty scaling and random prefix selection. A key open question is how reliably visible events track remaining credit as the policy evolves. Future work will examine this relationship across policy stages and develop prefix-based event predictors.
